title: Surowitz v. Hilton Hotels Corp. (1966)
summary: A derivative complaint was not a sham merely because the shareholder could not personally explain its detailed financial allegations.
notes: The opinion concerns the derivative verification requirement before the Court, rather than a general permission to sign allegations without a reasonable factual basis.

sections.Parties: Surowitz, a shareholder in Hilton Hotels, brought a derivative action alleging corporate wrongdoing.
sections.Material Facts: Surowitz had limited English and little formal education. Concern about her investment led her to rely on her son-in-law and others who investigated the company’s affairs over a substantial period. The resulting verified complaint was long and detailed. Her deposition revealed that she did not understand much of its technical content. The lower courts treated that inability as undermining the verification and the legitimacy of the action.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the complaint, and the court of appeals affirmed. The Supreme Court reversed.
sections.Issue: Did the shareholder’s lack of personal understanding of the detailed allegations justify dismissal under the derivative-action verification requirement?
sections.Holding: No. The record showed a genuine, investigated claim pursued in good faith rather than the sham litigation the requirement sought to prevent.
sections.Reasoning: The verification requirement served a protective function against unfounded derivative litigation. The Court assessed that purpose in light of the actual investigation and the plaintiff’s good-faith reliance on knowledgeable assistance. A requirement that every shareholder independently master complex corporate allegations would frustrate legitimate enforcement and exclude those who need professional help. The plaintiff’s inability to recite the complaint therefore did not establish bad faith or a basis to terminate the suit.

learning.why: A derivative complaint was not a sham merely because the shareholder could not personally explain its detailed financial allegations.

topics.cp-certification: A shareholder could rely in good faith on an informed investigation despite limited personal understanding of a complex complaint.
topics.cp-access: The Court rejected a treatment of verification that would exclude a genuine claim because of the plaintiff’s education or language limitations.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: The decision restored the opportunity to litigate without finding the alleged corporate fraud proven.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Harlan wrote separately concerning the supporting affidavit and the procedural basis for allowing the action to proceed.

mnemonic.rationale: A shareholder who did not understand her complaint
